transcript:
Meeting header: 2027-11-02 15:00 UTC | Duration ~52m | Attendees: Arielle (Redwood AE), Mateo (Redwood SE), Priya (Skyline Head of ML), Ethan (Platform), Maya (Security)

Summary: Quick intro, align POC success criteria and timeline; deep-dive on capacity sizing for reserved GPUs + burst/fallback plan; agree benchmark window and deliverables.

Topics: POC objectives, expected QPS & token profile, reserved capacity vs burst, autoscale guardrails, fallback policies, security/compliance gate, next steps.

00:00 Arielle: Hey everyone, thanks for doing this — appreciate you carving time. Quick round robin, then we want to sync on the POC scope: reserved capacity, autoscale and what graceful fallbacks look like.
00:18 Priya: Hi, I'm Priya. We run a recommendation ingestion pipeline and real-time prompt scoring; main ask is consistent p95 latency under peak load and predictable cost for first 3 months.
00:28 Ethan: Ethan here, i'll be the infra owner, so need the VPC/connectivity/egress details.
00:33 Maya: Maya — security and compliance. We'll need SOC2, SSO/SAML, KMS integration notes.
00:40 Arielle: Great. Mateo from our systems team will walk through runtime and how reserved GPUs + burst pool works. Mateo?
00:48 Mateo: Thanks. Quick tl;dr: Redwood offers reserved pools (dedicated GPUs) for steady throughput and a burst pool to handle spikes. For POC we typically recommend a small reserved commit that covers baseline 60-70% of expected sustained qps so you get the deterministic tail latency, and then burst handles ~2-4x short spikes. Fallbacks are policy-driven: prefer model-variant downgrade (e.g., quantized variant), regional fallback, or queued requests with a graceful retry.
01:15 Priya: Ok, our profile: average request 300 tokens in context, responses ~80 tokens. Peak traffic currently around 120 qps for scoring, but we want to plan for up to 300 qps during promotions. Target is p95 < 450ms for scoring path.
01:34 Mateo: That helps. For 300 qps at that token size we estimate ~X tokens/sec — let me call out numbers: 300 qps * 380 tokens = 114k tokens/sec. On A100-class hardware with current kernels, that's roughly N reserved GPUs depending on batching. For planning POC, propose reserving 4 GPUs and enabling burst up to 8 for short windows; we can run cost-limited burst.
02:05 Ethan: When you say 4 GPUs, is that for top-of-the-line V100/A100? We use G5 instances in our cloud.
02:12 Mateo: Good question. The model and quantization matter. If you're using an open LLM 7B quantized to 4-bit, the compute per token is much less vs 13B float. We should run a short profiling benchmark with your prompt set to pick GPU SKU and batch sizing.
02:33 Priya: We'll be using a fine-tuned 7B initially, might test a 13B later. For POC we can stick to 7B quantized.
02:40 Mateo: Perfect — that keeps burst costs modest. Regarding autoscale: Redwood autoscaler monitors queue depth, p95 latency, and token backlog. Policy example: maintain p95 <= 450ms; if p95 breaches for 2 consecutive minutes and queue length grows, add a burst node up to configured cap. Cooldown is 3 minutes to avoid thrash.
03:05 Priya: How do warm starts work? We can't afford cold-start spikes.
03:08 Mateo: Two approaches: keep a minimal warm pool (tiny fraction of reserved) and use prefix KV cache preload for popular prompts. The burst nodes can be kept in a prewarmed state when we expect promotions. For unexpected spikes, fallback to model-variant downgrade or graceful queueing with informative 429 + retry-after.
03:33 Ethan: What's the typical latency delta when we downgrade model-variant vs queue?
03:36 Mateo: Downgrading to a quantized smaller variant usually lowers latency by ~20-30% and cost by ~40%, depending on sequence length. Queueing keeps cost minimal but increases end-to-end latency predictably. We can do hybrid: for VIP traffic try model downgrade, for bulk async traffic queue.
03:57 Maya: For security, we need audit logs, per-request metadata, and KMS key wrap options. Are logs retained in your control plane?
04:06 Arielle: For Redwood Private we'd integrate with your KMS and you can choose log retention; for hosted we have SOC2 and provide audit logs export; we'll send the security pack.
04:18 Maya: Ok please include SAML metadata and applicable encryption in transit/at rest docs.

05:00 Mateo: Back to capacity math — quick back-of-envelope: with batching we typically achieve higher throughput, but latency SLO constrains max batch window. If your target p95 is 450ms, we need batch latency budget < 150ms. That limits batch sizes; so GPU count scales mostly linearly. For the benchmark we'll test several batch sizes (1,4,8) and measure latency distribution.
05:42 Priya: Good. For success criteria: p95 under 450ms for scoring flow for 95% of test windows; peak handoff during a 15-minute promo spike (300 qps) should not have more than 5% dropped/failed requests; cost per 1M tokens should be demonstrably cheaper than our current baseline by at least 10%.
06:12 Arielle: Nice concise success criteria. We'll put that in the SOW.
06:18 Ethan: How long does warmup take for a node? If burst nodes are cold, they'll add big latencies.
06:24 Mateo: Cold start can be 20-60s depending on model and io. That's why we recommend prewarmed burst and KV cache priming. For POC we can configure a prewarm schedule around your test windows.
06:40 Priya: Timeline? We want the POC done in ~6 weeks.
06:44 Arielle: Typical POC flow: week 0-1 kick off + infra provisioning + share traces, week 2 run profiling + pick GPU SKU, week 3 run load tests and iterate, week 4 prove fallback policies, week 5 soak test and security review, week 6 final results and decision. Is that reasonable?
07:02 Priya: Yes. We'll aim to share traces by Friday.

07:20 Mateo: For the benchmarking harness we'll do two main tests: steady-state throughput at target qps and a spike test (15 minute promotion simulation) with traffic ramps to 300 qps. We'll collect p50/p95/p99, token/sec, GPU util, queue depth. Also model variant toggles to measure fallback outcomes.
07:45 Ethan: Who runs the spike tests? We can run from our infra or Redwood can run from hosted.
07:50 Arielle: We suggest Redwood runs the first baseline so configs are validated; then we hand over the harness so Skyline can rerun in your cloud if desired. We'll provide the load generator and step-by-step.
08:02 Priya: Sounds good. A couple of questions about billing — if we reserve 4 GPUs but burst to 8 for a short window, how is that billed?
08:10 Arielle: Reserved is monthly commit; burst is usage-based on top with cap set in SOW. For POC we often do a time-boxed burst budget to avoid surprises. We'll include an example cost table in the SOW.
08:25 Maya: Compliance — anything that makes this unsuitable for PII? We have redacted input in scoring, but still need assurances.
08:32 Arielle: We'll provide the Private deployment option if needed; for hosted we have data retention controls and encryption. We'll include the data flow diagram and options.

08:55 Mateo: I want to call out one architectural fallback we use that's a bit different: traffic hedging. For certain priority requests, we can fan-out to two model-variants in parallel and return the fastest response, or we can use a speculative small-model preview that returns a quick approximate score and then reconcile. That reduces tail latency at cost of doubling compute for hedged requests.
09:22 Priya: Interesting — might be useful for VIP users. We'll need to see cost tradeoffs.

09:40 Ethan: Any examples of autoscaler oscillation? We don't want the system thrashing during noisy traffic.
09:44 Mateo: We mitigate with cooldown, smoothing window, and minimum up-time per burst node. We also put a priority on model-variant downgrade before spinning up too many nodes.
09:56 Priya: For the benchmark dataset, should we anonymize or provide a synthetic throughput trace?
10:01 Mateo: Either works; real traces are better for KV cache hit patterns. If you're uncomfortable, provide anonymized traces and a couple of representative prompts.
10:12 Priya: We'll share anonymized traces.

10:28 Arielle: Recap quick: SOW + pricing by Thursday; traces and prompts by Friday; Redwood to provide benchmark harness by Monday; run baseline and spike tests next week; follow-up 11/16 to review.
10:45 Priya: Agreed.

11:00 Mateo: One more nit — for reserved sizing we can give you two options: conservative (50% of peak reserved, cheaper but more bursting) or aggressive (cover 80-90% of peak, higher commit but fewer burst charges). For POC we recommend conservative to validate burst behavior, then adjust.
11:23 Ethan: Conservative makes sense for us initially.

11:35 Maya: Also include data residency notes in the SOW — some of our customers are EU-only.
11:40 Arielle: Will do.

End: Final recap of action items and next steps.
